slides.title: Select Characteristics of Sole Proprietorship
slides.text:
Select Characteristics of Sole Proprietorship
Formalities and Regulations: There are minimum formalities and regulations. Even the auditing of financial statement is not necessary, but balance sheet could be useful for seeking a bank loan.
Depending on the state and city, it may be required to register with local government. Most local governments do not require registration, but some do
Taxation: Sole proprietor is taxed individually and the business is not taxed separately. Therefore, owner is responsible for paying income tax on the income earned from sole proprietorship, in his personal capacity.
Continuity: There is no perpetual continuity of this form of business entity as it gets dissolved with the death of the entrepreneur.

Business Licenses in India
Trade License: To ensure that the manner in which a business is being carried on is according to the relevant rules, standards and safety guidelines the municipal authority in charge of the place where trade is conducted issues a Trade License.
Employee Provident Fund Registration: With the Employee Provident Fund Organization. Mandatory, if more than 20 employees.
Employee State Insurance (ESI) Registration: Mandatory if 10 employees in a factory or 20 in other establishments
Compulsory industrial license: under the provisions of Industrial (D&R) Act, 1951: For, Distillation and brewing of alcoholic drinks, Cigars and cigarettes of tobacco and manufactured tobacco substitutes; Electronic Aerospace and defense equipment, all types; Industrial explosives, including detonating fuses, safety fuses, gun powder, nitrocellulose and matches; Hazardous chemicals

slides.title: Locational Restrictions
slides.text:
Locational Restrictions
The location of industrial units is subject to applicable local zoning and land use regulations and environmental regulations.
Industrial license is required if the proposed location of the unit is within 25 km of standard urban area limits of 23 cities having a population of one million as per 1991 Census.
The restriction does not apply: If the unit were to be located in an area designated as an “industrial area” before the 25th July, 1991. In the case of Electronics, Computer software and Printing and any other industry, notified in future as “non polluting industry”.

slides.title: Environmental Clearance
slides.text:
Environmental Clearance
Promoters of projects, subject to conditions, are required to obtain statutory clearances relating to Pollution Control and Environment as may be necessary, for setting up an industrial project belonging to specified categories as amended from time to time, by the Ministry of Environment & Forests under The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.
Setting up industries in certain locations, considered ecologically fragile, is guided by separate guidelines issued by the Ministry of Environment and Forests.

slides.title: Import Export License
slides.text:
Import Export License
India allows for free import of most of the goods however some categories of products are strictly prohibited and some are allowed conditional import under import license. Import License is issued by the Director General of Foreign Trade (DGFT).
Typically the license is valid for 24 months for capital goods and 18 months for raw materials, components, spare parts and consumables.
An Import License consists of two copies.
Foreign Exchange Control Copy: To be utilized for effecting remittance to foreign seller or for opening letter of credit
Customs Copy: To be utilized for presenting to Customs authority enabling them to clear the goods.
Application for Export License must be submitted to the Director General of Foreign Trade (DGFT).
Importer Exporter Code: From Director General of Foreign Trade

slides.title: Partnership:
slides.text:
Partnership:
Partnership is a type of lawful business wherein two or more than two people (not more than fifty) have a legal relationship and voluntarily combine their capital to run a lawful business with a profit motive by oral or written agreement.
They share the profits and losses of the business in mutually agreed proportions as decided and written in the partnership deed with unlimited liability.
The partnership has no continuity, if one partner dies, retires or is declared insolvent, the entire enterprise must be dissolved.
There is a restriction on transfer of interest or share by a partner without the consent of other partners.
Auditing the financial statements is not necessary. It is not mandatory to form a balance sheet, although it is advisable to do so for financial clarity and raising of a loan.

slides.title: Contents of a Written Partnership Deed
slides.text:
Contents of a Written Partnership Deed
Name of the partnership firm.
The names of the partners.
Permanent address of the partnership.
Duration of the partnership.
Nature of the business to be carried out by partnership firm and its aims and objectives.
Rights, powers and duties of different partners.
Decisions about financial year end and maintenance of accounting records.
Extent of contribution of each partner in the partnership firm.
Proportion in which profits and losses are to be divided amongst partners.
Name of the person(s) who have the authority to manage the partnership firm and have the authority to sign the cheques.
The nature of division of tasks between the partners.
Arbitration clause, in case of any dispute/disagreement amongst partners.
Procedure with respect to the dissolution of the partnership firm.

slides.title: Joint Stock Company:
slides.text:
Joint Stock Company:
It has evolved as a voluntary association of persons who contribute their capital as members or shareholders of the company.
All undertakings incorporated and registered as per Companies Act are termed as ‘companies’.
Company is an artificial person created by law, having a separate legal entity, with perpetual succession and common seal.
“A corporation is an artificial being, invisible, intangible and existing only in contemplation of the law. Being a mere creation of law, it possesses only the properties which the charter of its creation centers upon it either expressly or as incidental to its very existence. (Chief Justice Marshall)
The life and existence of the company is not dependent on life of its member. It is created by the process of law and can be put to an end only by a process duly established by the law.

slides.text:
As all the shareholders of the company may not participate with the functioning of the business they elect their representative known as ‘Board of Directors’, who are responsible for managing and exercising the rights and responsibilities of the business organization through hiring the senior management of the organization.
Publication of Financial Results: It is obligatory for a joint stock company to file its annual report with the registrar of companies at the end of year.
Independent Directors: In order to ensure the empowerment and effectiveness of the board to manage the companies, government has made it mandatory for the companies to institute independent directors with lot of authority and corresponding accountability.
Every listed public company must have at least one-third of its total board of directors comprised of independent directors. Under SEBI LODR regulations, if the regular Chairperson of the Board is an executive director or related to the promoters, it is at least half (50%) of the board
Independent Non-executive Directors are outsiders who have judgment and logic, are articulate, can bring fresh ideas and, above all, act as a watchdog to safeguard stakeholders’ (shareholders, suppliers and customers) interests from an overzealous management.

slides.visual_text: Heading: One Person Company. A silhouette of a man in a suit with six arrows. Cost to Register: almost the same as Private Limited Company, a bit lower. slides.title: Private Ltd Co.
slides.text:
Private Ltd Co.
Prohibits any invitation to the public to subscribe for any shares or debentures or deposits from persons other than its members, directors or their relatives.
It must have a minimum paid up capital of one lakh rupees or such higher paid-up capital as may be prescribed, and by its articles. There are two to two hundred shareholders.
Name of the company must end with suffix “Pvt. Ltd”.
Shares of these companies are not traded upon in open market and are only held by the directors and the company members.
Liability of the shareholders is limited to an extent equal to their investment.
Requires Memorandum of Association, Articles of Association and Certificate of Incorporation to commence with business.

slides.title: Public Limited Company:
slides.text:
Public Limited Company:
It has the minimum paid-up capital of five lakh rupees or such higher paid up capital, as may be prescribed.
It can be formed with minimum of seven members and there is no limit for maximum number of members.
Its shares can be traded in the open market on the stock exchanges on which these companies are listed.
It can raise part of its capital through public offering of its shares.
It can be taken over by another company through the act of purchasing a controlling interest in the overall share holding of the company.
The shares of the company are easily transferable and they can invite people for subscription of shares and debentures.
They are required to issue prospectus prior to raising the capital. It’s their obligation to allot the shares within 120 day’s from the issue of prospectus.
They use the word “Limited” as suffix.
The public limited company can start business only after the issue of the certificate of commencement of the business by the Registrar of companies.

slides.title: Holding Company
slides.text:
Holding Company
Controls the composition of board of directors of another company; or
Holds more than half of the nominal value of equity share capital of another company.
The company which is controlled is called subsidiary company.
A company is said to be subsidiary company if the formation of its board of directors is controlled by other company. This controlling company has the majority of its voting rights or the maximum number of shares for the control of the company.

slides.title: Formation of a Company
slides.text:
Formation of a Company
Members may form an incorporated company for a lawful purpose by subscribing their names (putting their signatures) to the Memorandum of Association (MoA) and complying with the requirements in respect of registration.
MoA means an agreement between the persons concerned to associate themselves into a body corporate.
The application for registration of a company with the required documents has to be submitted to the Registrar of Companies of the state in which the registered office of the company is to be established.
Certificate of Incorporation: From the date of incorporation, the company gets the legal effects of separate legal identity, perpetual succession, and common seal etc.
Commencement of Business: A private company may commence its business immediately after its incorporation but a public company cannot commence business immediately after incorporation unless it has obtained a certificate of commencement from the Registrar.

slides.title: Memorandum of Association
slides.text:
Memorandum of Association
“The purpose of the memorandum is to enable the shareholders, creditors and those who deal with the company, to know its permitted range of enterprise.” - Lord Macmillan.
It is a printed document divided into different paragraphs as different clauses.
It is signed by each subscriber along with their name, address, description and occupation.
It is signed in presence of at least one witness, who sign along with his name, address, description and occupation
MoA comprises of different clauses defining the nature and scope of the organization.
This document is basic and mandatory for each company and a fundamental part of the constitution of a company.
It can be altered but subject to certain conditions.
It is a public document & is open for inspection of those who deal with Co.
It forms the basis for relationship of company with outsiders.

slides.title: Clauses of MoA
slides.text:
Clauses of MoA
Name Clause: This clause specifies the name of the company and provides guideline with respect to how to name a company. It states that:
Name of the company must be published and displayed.
There is restriction on using undesirable (identical) and inappropriate name for a company.
Registered Office Clause: It specifies the address of the registered office and the head office of an organization
Legal documents and books of a company are kept at RO and notices are served from this office.
It is not necessary that RO of the company is principal place of business i.e. it can be different from the operational field.

slides.title: Clauses of MoA
slides.text:
Clauses of MoA
Object Clause: It defines the purpose for which a company has been incorporated.
This clause informs the members how company will use their capital.
It is divided into two parts: Main object and Incidental or Ancillary objects. Main object defines the basic purpose for which a company is created. Incidental or Ancillary objects are the allied activities that it has to undertake to perform the activities listed in the object clause.
It defines the scope of operations of a company.
To inform creditors and outsiders about the rights of company (in case of ultra-virus acts).
It also defines the restricted objects for which a company cannot be formed like: immoral, illegal, or activities that are opposed to public policy or which violate the provisions of Indian Companies Act.

It is divided into two parts: Main object and Incidental or Ancillary objects. Main object defines the basic purpose for which a company is created. Incidental or Ancillary objects are the allied activities that it has to undertake to perform the activities listed in the object clause.
It defines the scope of operations of a company.
To inform creditors and outsiders about the rights of company (in case of ultra-virus acts).

It also defines the restricted objects for which a company cannot be formed like: immoral, illegal, or activities that are opposed to public policy or which violate the provisions of Indian Companies Act.

slides.title: Clauses of MoA
slides.text:
Clauses of MoA
Liability Clause: The liability of the company can be limited by shares or by guarantee.
But, under the following circumstances the privilege with respect to limited liability can be withdrawn and members can be forced to be fully liable to repay the due liabilities of a company:
Company willfully defrauds creditors.
Number of members reduces below the minimum number and company carries on business for more than 6 months with this reduced number.
Share Capital Clause: It specifies the composition of the authorized capital of the company with its division into fixed denomination shares.
Authorized capital is the maximum limit up to which a company can issue shares.
Association or Subscription Clause: Declaration of Association by signatories.
Due attestation by the witness
Desire to form company and subscription to shares.

slides.title: Winding up of a Company
slides.text:
Winding up of a Company
A company can be wound up only by adopting the procedure laid out by law.
Voluntary winding up initiated by resolution of the company in general meeting. It can be of two types:
Members’ voluntary winding up
Creditors voluntary Winding up
Winding up under the supervision of the Court.
Compulsory winding up by the court initiated by petition to the Court:
1. Special resolution by the board at AGM
2. Default in filing statutory report, or holding statutory meeting
3. Failure to commence business within specified time
4. Reduction of membership below the stated minimum number
5. Inability of the company to repay its debts

(A). Under Statutory Provisions
Where company is a mere sham and the device of incorporation is used for illegal or improper use to do fraud.
Where company is incorporated for evading contractual and statutory obligations.
Where a company is used to evade tax.

slides.title: Cooperative Societies: Indian Co-operative Societies Act 1912
slides.text:
Cooperative Societies: Indian Co-operative Societies Act 1912
It is run by the members who are generally from a common background for protecting or enhancing their interest through a cooperative effort.
The members decide to come together under the banner of single organization with a belief that individually they will not be able to protect their commercial interests, because of lack of: scale, competencies and resources.
Co-operative societies are the religiously neutral voluntary foundations where different people combine their capital in order to serve the members of the society rather than to create profits, as there is inadequate amount of capital with the individual members of the society.
And they are likely to share the benefits like limited liability and perpetual succession by coming together as cooperative.
In India such societies have been started to promote the welfare of the weaker classes of society.
Through these corporations, government also tries to contribute to the development of the people at the bottom of the pyramid. Therefore, these societies sometimes have some form of governmental control as well.

slides.title: There are three pertinent legal forms of not-for-profit entities under Indian law:
slides.text:
There are three pertinent legal forms of not-for-profit entities under Indian law:
Trusts
Societies
Section 8 companies
There are no restrictions on Indian NPOs’ business/commercial/ economic activities. However, the profits must be applied fully towards charitable objects.
If this is not done, then the NPO will lose its income tax exemption and its income will be liable to tax at the maximum marginal rate (35.1%).
Further the NPO must maintain separate books of account for the business/commercial/economic activities.

slides.title: Trusts
slides.text:
Trusts
It is a form of not-for-profit entity in India.
It can be established for relief of poverty, education, medical relief, provision of facilities for recreation, and any other object of general public utility.
Public charitable trusts, as distinguished from private trusts, are designed to benefit members of an uncertain and fluctuating class.
In determining whether a trust is public or private, the key question is whether the class to be benefited constitutes a substantial segment of the public.
It must register with the office of the Charity Commissioner of the state in order to be eligible to apply for tax-exemption.
Indian public trusts are generally irrevocable.
No national law governs public charitable trusts in India, although many states (Maharashtra, Gujarat, Rajasthan, & MP) have Public Trusts Acts.
A trust of immoveable property can be created by either a non-testamentary document and another by a testamentary document such as a will.
A trust regarding an immoveable property cannot be created orally but it must be by a document duly registered.

slides.title: At least two trustees are required to register a public charitable trust.
slides.text:
At least two trustees are required to register a public charitable trust.
Legal title of the property of a public charitable trust vests in trustees
Trustees of a public charitable trust may not, however, in any way use trust property or their position for their own interest or private advantage.
Trustees may not enter into agreements in which they may have a personal interest that conflicts or may possibly conflict with the interests of the beneficiaries of the trust (whose interests the trustees are bound to protect).
Trustees may not delegate any of their duties, functions or powers to a co-trustee or any other person, except that trustees may delegate ministerial acts.
In essence, trustees may not delegate authority with respect to duties requiring the exercise of discretion.

If it becomes too difficult to carry out the objects of a trust, the doctrine of cypres, meaning "as near as possible," may be applied to change the objects of the trust.

slides.title: Societies
slides.text:
Societies
Societies are membership organizations that may be registered for charitable purposes.
Societies are usually managed by a governing council or a managing committee.
Societies are governed by the Societies Registration Act 1860, which has been adapted by various states.
A minimum of seven individuals are required to form a society.
The applicants must register the society with the state Registrar of Societies having jurisdiction in order to be eligible to apply for tax-exempt status.
A registration application includes the society's memorandum of association and rules and regulations.

slides.text:
The governance of societies also differs from that of trusts; societies are usually managed by a governing council or managing committee, whereas trusts are governed by their trustees.
Individuals or institutions or both may be members of a society.
The general body of members delegates the management of day-to-day affairs to the managing committee, which is usually elected by the members.
Members of the general body of the society have voting rights and can demand the submission of accounts and the annual report of the society for inspection.
Members of the managing committee may hold office for such period of time as may be specified under the bylaws of the society.

slides.text:
Societies, unlike trusts, must file annually, with the Register of Societies, a list of the names, addresses and occupations of their managing committee members.
In a society, all property is held in the name of the society, whereas all of the property of a trust legally vests in the trustees.
Unlike trusts, societies may be dissolved.
Dissolution must be approved by at least three-fifths of the society's members.
Upon dissolution, and after settlement of all debts and liabilities, the funds and property of the society may not be distributed among the members of the society.
The remaining funds and property must be given or transferred to some other society, preferably one with similar objects as the dissolved entity.

slides.title: Sec. 8 Company
slides.text:
Sec. 8 Company
The Indian Companies Act, permits certain companies to obtain not-for-profit status as "section 8 companies."
It is formed for "promoting commerce, art, science, religion, charity or any other useful object," provided that no profits, if any, or other income derived through promoting the company's objects may be distributed in any form to its members.
At least three individuals are required to form it.
The founders or promoters must submit application materials to the Regional Director of the Company Law Board.
The application must include copies of the memorandum and articles of association of the proposed company, as well as a statement of assets and a brief description of the work proposed to be done upon registration.

slides.title: Sec. 8 Company
slides.text:
Sec. 8 Company
Its internal governance is similar to that of a society.
It generally has members and is governed by directors or a managing committee or a governing council elected by its members.
Like a society (but unlike a trust), a Section 8 company may be dissolved.
Upon dissolution and after settlement of all debts and liabilities, the funds and property of the company may not be distributed among the members of the company.
The remaining funds and property must be given or transferred to some other Section 8 company, preferably one having similar objects as the dissolved entity.

slides.title: Public Benefit Status
slides.text:
Public Benefit Status
To be eligible for tax-exemption under the Income Tax Act, 1961, Amended By Finance Act, 2024, a not-for-profit entity must be organized for religious or charitable purposes.
Charitable purposes include "relief of the poor, education, medical relief and the advancement of any other object of general public utility."
Public charitable trusts, by definition, must be created for the benefit of the public.
Societies likewise may be registered for charitable purposes.
Section 8 companies are formed for the limited purposes of "promoting commerce, art, science, religion, charity or any other useful object."

slides.title: Organizations may qualify for tax-exempt status if the following conditions are met:
slides.text:
Organizations may qualify for tax-exempt status if the following conditions are met:
It must be organized for religious or charitable purposes;
It must spend 85% of its income in any financial year (April 1st to March 31st) on the objects of the organization.
It has until 12 months following the end of the financial year to comply with this requirement.
Surplus income may be accumulated for specific projects for a period ranging from 1 to 5 years;
No part of the income or property of the organization may be used or applied directly or indirectly for the benefit of the founder, trustee, relative of the founder or trustee or a person who has contributed in excess of Rs. 50,000 to the organization in a financial year
The organization must timely file its annual income return.
